title: Sourcing and Automation of Political News and Information over Social Media in the United States, 2016-2018
screen_reason: Observational content-sharing study of Twitter. 21.8m political-hashtag tweets were collected across two US events; every shared base URL was hand-coded against a grounded source typology, and the paper reports the share of shared URLs that came from 'Junk News and Information' domains, i.e. 'sources that deliberately publish misleading, deceptive, or incorrect information packaged as real news'. That is a quantitative share of shared links attributable to an unreliable-source class, with a stated denominator, for two separate data-collection periods -- eligible SHARING (content_share) under the source-level-list branch of the inclusion rule. The paper additionally reports a top-activity group of accounts and its share of divisive and conspiracy sharing, which is an eligible CONCENTRATION estimate.

estimates.measure_type: % of URL-carrying tweets in the US presidential election hashtag sample whose shared source was coded Junk News and Information
estimates.denominator: 2,792,760 URL-carrying tweets collected from Twitter's streaming API on 45+ US presidential election hashtags, 1-9 November 2016 (all coded categories, including non-political 'Other' content, are in the total)
estimates.definition: The first URL shared in the tweet resolved to a base URL that coders had labelled 'Junk News and Information', meaning the domain satisfied at least three of five criteria: professionalism, style, credibility, bias, counterfeit
estimates.misinfo_def: "We developed the concept of 'junk news,' which refers to sources that deliberately publish misleading, deceptive, or incorrect information packaged as real news."
estimates.page_loc: Table 2, 'Political news and information shared on Twitter, 2016-2018', p. 12 (Presidential Election columns)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Six trained coders (election wave) at the Oxford Internet Institute manually labelled 710 base URLs against a five-criteria grounded typology (professionalism, style, credibility, bias, counterfeit; at least three required for junk news), inspecting About pages, at least five front-page stories, WHOIS and Wikipedia, and consulting third-party fact-checkers (PolitiFact, Snopes, Media Bias/Fact Check, Politico). Krippendorff's alpha = 0.89, measured on random sets of 50 sources; non-consensus cases re-evaluated in face-to-face meetings, one core team member adjudicated highly ambiguous cases; over 1,000 hours of coding, six training sessions, 22 months of iterative typology development. Domain labels were then applied to individual links by a Python script.
estimates.moderator_quote: In total, we collected 19.53 million tweets about the presidential election and 2.26 million tweets about the SOTU address. ... Overall, we extracted 3.26 million URLs about the presidential election and 145,000 about the SOTU address. If Twitter users shared more than one URL in their tweet, only the first URL was analyzed.
estimates.notes: Classification is at the level of the DOMAIN, not the individual story ('Rather than assessing the accuracy of individual stories that users shared, our grounded typology distinguishes different types of news and information domains'), hence classification_level source_level and breadth left blank. The denominator is the Table 2 column total of 2,792,760, which is smaller than the 3.26m URLs the methods say were extracted; the paper does not reconcile the two figures (uncodable or dropped links are the likely gap). Table 3 gives a marginally different divisive/professional total (617,797 and 674,212 vs 617,660 and 674,269 in Table 2); the Table 2 figures are used here because they carry the percentage. Time series in Table 3 collapsed to this single aggregate point per the one-representative-point rule.

estimates.denominator: 116,380 URL-carrying tweets collected from Twitter's streaming API on four State of the Union hashtags (#SOTU, #stateoftheunion, #SOTU2018, #stateoftheunionaddress), 24-30 January 2018
estimates.definition: The first URL shared in the tweet resolved to a base URL that coders had labelled 'Junk News and Information', meaning the domain satisfied at least three of five criteria: professionalism, style, credibility, bias, counterfeit
estimates.misinfo_def: "We developed the concept of 'junk news,' which refers to sources that deliberately publish misleading, deceptive, or incorrect information packaged as real news."
estimates.page_loc: Table 2, 'Political news and information shared on Twitter, 2016-2018', p. 12 (State of the Union columns)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Five trained coders (SOTU wave) applied the same five-criteria grounded typology to the 710 hand-labelled base URLs; Krippendorff's alpha = 0.89 reported for the US coding overall; third-party fact-checkers (PolitiFact, Snopes, Media Bias/Fact Check) and WHOIS/Wikipedia used as corroborating sources; ambiguous cases adjudicated by a core team member.
estimates.moderator_quote: For the SOTU address, our team identified only four event-specific hashtags that generated substantial traffic on Twitter.
estimates.notes: Same corpus construction and coding as the 2016 row, different event and period, so split per the one-row-per-measure rule. The SOTU denominator (116,380 in Table 2) is again smaller than the 145,000 URLs the methods report extracting. Table 4's daily totals (34,740 professional, 20,984 divisive) differ slightly from Table 2's (34,963 and 21,219).

estimates.measure_type: % of URL-carrying tweets in the US presidential election hashtag sample whose shared source fell in the broader Divisive and Conspiracy Sources category (junk news + WikiLeaks + Russian state-linked sources)
estimates.denominator: 2,792,760 URL-carrying tweets collected from Twitter's streaming API on 45+ US presidential election hashtags, 1-9 November 2016
estimates.definition: The shared base URL was labelled in the parent category Divisive and Conspiracy Sources, comprising the subcategories Junk News and Information, WikiLeaks, and Russia (Russia Today, Sputnik, Guccifer 2.0)
estimates.misinfo_def: "The third category, Divisive and Conspiracy Content, included various forms of unreliable and deceptive sources."
estimates.page_loc: Table 2, Divisive and Conspiracy Sources subtotal row, p. 12 (Presidential Election columns)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same six-coder OII typology exercise as the junk news row (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.89). The WikiLeaks subcategory was placed here because 'the page repeatedly promoted conspiracy theories about Hillary Clinton and the Democratic Party'; the Russia subcategory 'was constituted exclusively of links to the government-funded Russia Today, Sputnik, and the Russian-hacker Guccifer 2.0' and was included 'due to their known slanted reporting and application of propaganda techniques'.
estimates.moderator_quote: The third category, Divisive and Conspiracy Content, included various forms of unreliable and deceptive sources. The most important subcategory here was labeled Junk News and Information.
estimates.notes: definition_variant=true: this is the BROADER definition of the same 2016 country x platform cell whose narrow reading is the 17.4% junk news row; do not pool the two. The subtotal is printed verbatim by the authors in Table 2, so it is not a sum I computed (R8 satisfied), but borderline=true because two of its three components stretch the misinformation construct: WikiLeaks links are authentic leaked documents placed in the category for the site's conspiracy promotion, and the Russia subcategory is a state-media provenance label rather than a falsity judgement. An adjudicator who wants a strictly falsity-based numerator should keep only the 17.4% row.

estimates.moderator_quote: During the SOTU address, the proportion decreased to roughly 1:1.7 as the proportion of professional sources grew from 22.1 percent to 30.0 percent.
estimates.notes: Broader definition variant of the 18.1% junk news row for the same 2018 cell; in 2018 the WikiLeaks (3 tweets) and Russia (145 tweets) components are negligible, so the broad and narrow values nearly coincide. Same borderline caveat as the 2016 broad row.

estimates.measure_type: share of all divisive and conspiracy source shares that came from high-volume amplifier accounts (0.11% of users)
estimates.value_raw: 4,165 amplifier accounts of 3.69m users (0.11%) generated 180,337 divisive and conspiracy shares, "27.8 percent of all tweets in this category"
estimates.conc_group_label: Amplifier accounts: accounts posting 50 or more times a day using the study's election hashtags (automated, semiautomated, or highly active human-curated)
estimates.denominator: conc_group_pct denominator: 3.69m Twitter users in the 2016 election hashtag sample (Table 1). conc_share_pct denominator: all tweets sharing Divisive and Conspiracy Sources in that sample (674,269 per Table 2).
estimates.definition: An account qualified as an amplifier if it posted at least 50 times per day using one of the selected hashtags during the collection period; its tweets counted toward the numerator when the shared source was in the Divisive and Conspiracy Sources category
estimates.misinfo_def: "We developed the concept of 'junk news,' which refers to sources that deliberately publish misleading, deceptive, or incorrect information packaged as real news."
estimates.source_quote: For Polarizing and Conspiracy Content, the number of total shares almost doubled to 180,337 shares generating 27.8 percent of all tweets in this category.
estimates.page_loc: p. 15, 'Amplified Political Communication across Two Political Events in the US'; group size from Table 5 and Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Amplifier status assigned by a volume threshold (50+ tweets/day on the study hashtags), not by a bot classifier; the authors note the threshold was set because 'we have identified very few human users that tweeted more than 49.5 times on average per day' and that 'more complex methods using machine learning yield comparative numbers of positives'. The content side uses the same 710-domain hand-coded typology (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.89).
estimates.moderator_quote: We identified amplifier accounts as those that posted 50 times a day or more using one of the selected hashtags during the data collection period.
estimates.notes: TWO CAVEATS FOR THE ADJUDICATOR. (1) conc_group_pct is not stated by the authors; it is an exact part/whole share from two verbatim counts with the same denominator -- 4,165 amplifier accounts (Table 5) out of the 3.69m users in the same election sample (Table 1) = 0.11% -- which R8 permits, but the paper never frames the accounts as a 'top X%'. (2) The authors' own 27.8% does not reproduce from their tables: 180,337 / 674,269 = 26.7% (and 180,337 / 674,212 using Table 3's total = 26.7%). The companion professional-news figure does reproduce (95,385 / 617,660 = 15.4%, reported as 15.5%), so the 27.8% looks like an error; note that 27.8 is also the Table 2 subtotal percentage for the unrelated 'Other Political News and Information' category. The verbatim 27.8 is kept per R8, but 26.7 may be the correct value. The 2018 counterpart is not extractable: only 15 amplifier accounts were found, generating 14 divisive-content tweets, and the authors give only 'driving only 0.3 percent of the total traffic' for all traffic, not for misinformation.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED, available if an adjudicator wants finer source classes: the two other subcategories inside Divisive and Conspiracy Sources are reported separately in Table 2 and could each be a narrower definition variant -- WikiLeaks 148,366 tweets (5.3%) in 2016 and 3 tweets (0.0%) in 2018; Russia 39,457 tweets (1.4%) in 2016 and 145 tweets (0.1%) in 2018. I left them out under R4 because neither is a falsity judgement (WikiLeaks hosts authentic leaked material; the Russia subcategory is a state-media provenance label), and because they are already inside the broad 24.1%/18.2% rows. Note a text/table conflict on the Russia figure: the narrative says the SOTU share was '.01 percent' while Table 2 reports 0.1. NOT EXTRACTED, ineligible: the professional-news amplifier figure (95,385 shares, 15.5% of that category) is not misinformation; the day-by-day series in Tables 3 and 4 was collapsed to the aggregate per the time-series rule (the 2016 divisive series runs 5.2% to 15.5% of daily shares, peaking at 104,574 URLs the day before the election, and would give a range_not_point row at best); the headline '1:1 ratio of junk news to professionally produced news' is a ratio between two categories, not a share of a denominator, and the derived 'share of professional voices ... increased by 17.5 percent across categories' is a difference of percentages; the 710 hand-coded base URLs are the coding frame, and the paper never reports how many of the 710 were junk news, so no source-level prevalence (share of DOMAINS that were junk) can be extracted; Table 5's amplifier tweet counts for 2018 (15 accounts, 6,945 tweets, 1,478 URLs, 14 divisive) carry no percentage. DENOMINATOR UNCERTAINTY worth an adjudicator's eye: Table 2's totals (2,792,760 and 116,380) are noticeably below the URL counts in the methods (3.26m and 145,000), and the Table 2 denominator includes 24.0% / 13.9% of clearly non-political 'Other' content (shopping, link shorteners, spam, social media platform links). A reviewer who wanted junk news as a share of POLITICAL news only would get a substantially higher figure, but the paper never reports that restricted denominator, so computing it is barred by R8. Finally, the coding is source-level over a 1 percent streaming-API sample of hashtag-selected tweets, so these values describe the hashtag conversation, not Twitter as a whole.

rob.design: Two real-time Twitter streaming-API collections on manually selected hashtag sets: 19.53m tweets / 3.69m users over 45+ election hashtags, 1-9 November 2016, and 2.26m tweets / 532,000 users over four SOTU hashtags, 24-30 January 2018; 3.26m and 145,000 URLs extracted, first URL per tweet only, shorteners unwrapped, tweet-to-tweet URLs dropped. Sampling frame is keyword/hashtag-selected and non-probability; the authors acknowledge the streaming API returns roughly 1 percent of public tweets and that Twitter's user base is not representative. Classification is at domain level: 710 base URLs hand-coded by six (2016) and five (2018) trained coders against a five-criteria grounded typology developed over 22 months, with third-party fact-checkers, WHOIS and Wikipedia as inputs; Krippendorff's alpha = 0.89 measured on random 50-source sets, disagreements resolved in team meetings and by a single adjudicator. Amplifier status rests on a simple 50-tweets-per-day volume threshold rather than a validated bot classifier, and the authors state they cannot attribute amplifier accounts to any actor. No response-rate concept applies. Main risks: hashtag selection, source-level rather than story-level truth assessment, an unreconciled gap between the extracted URL counts and the tabulated totals, and an arithmetic inconsistency in the amplifier percentage.
rob.item6_quote: A source was labeled as junk news when it satisfied at least three out our five criteria (professionalism; style; credibility; bias; and counterfeit).
